title: Isolated singularities and their classification
section: Complex Variables ▷ Singularities, Poles, and Laurent Series
terms: singularity; isolated singularity; punctured disk; removable singularity; pole; order of a pole; simple pole; double pole; essential singularity.

exposition.text:
An isolated singularity at a means the function is holomorphic on some punctured disk 0 <
|z − a| < R. It is removable if the function extends holomorphically across a, a pole of order m if
m
(z − a) f (z) extends with a nonzero value at a, and essential if neither case holds.
A removable singularity has no negative Laurent powers; a pole has finitely many, ending in
−m
(z − a) ; an essential singularity has infinitely many negative powers in the local punctured-disk
expansion. This classification must use an expansion centered at the singularity and valid near
it, not an exterior annulus centered elsewhere.
A simple pole has order one and a double pole has order two. A bounded holomorphic function
near an isolated missing point has a removable singularity. If other singularities accumulate
at the point, no punctured disk of holomorphy exists, and the isolated-singularity trichotomy
cannot be used.

question.text:
Consider f(z) = 1/ sin(1/z) at points where it is defined near zero. Which description of z = 0
is correct?
(A) A removable isolated singularity.
(B) A simple pole.
(C) An essential isolated singularity.
(D) A pole of infinite order.
(E) A nonisolated singular point, because poles accumulate at zero.

solution.text:
For every nonzero integer k, the point z = 1/(kπ) makes sin(1/z) = 0. These are poles,
since the derivative of the denominator there is nonzero, and they accumulate at zero.
There is therefore no punctured disk about zero on which f is holomorphic. The remov-
able/pole/essential trichotomy for isolated singularities does not apply.

(A) Essential (B) Removable
(C) A pole of order three (D) A simple pole
(E) A pole of order two

solution.text:
The numerator has a simple zero at 1/2, since its derivative there is −π sin(π/2) = −π ̸= 0.
One of the denominator’s two zero factors cancels, leaving a simple pole.
